questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Kinds of AI systems
questions.question: A port operator's IS auditor is told its berth-scheduling tool uses AI. Which evidence would BEST show that it is a machine-learning model rather than a rules engine?

options.A: Logs showing berths are assigned without any planner approving them
options.B: Training records drawn from the port's past berthing data
options.C: Test results showing identical inputs produce identical schedules
options.D: Vendor documentation describing the tool as an AI-powered scheduler

questions.key_concept: Machine learning is defined by logic learned from data, not by automation or marketing labels; the type decides which evidence the auditor needs.
questions.pre_read: Before reading the options, ask what actually separates software that learns from software that follows written rules.
questions.correct_explanation: Machine learning means the logic was learned from data, so records of the data the tool was trained on show directly how its logic was made, and bring training data, validation and drift into scope. Vendor documentation, option D, is the runner-up: it is a useful pointer, but an AI label is a claim, and rules software is often marketed as AI too.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because AI is often linked with automation. But rules engines also decide without approval; automation raises an oversight question, not a question of type.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because repeatable output sounds technical. But fixed rules and many deployed models both repeat outputs for the same inputs, so this cannot separate them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the vendor knows its product. But an AI label is a claim, not evidence of how the logic was made; rules software is often marketed as AI.

tips: Eliminate: A shows automation, which rules engines also provide, and C shows repeatable output, which fixed rules and many deployed models share.
Final two: B beats D because records of training data show the logic was learned; a vendor's AI label is a claim, and rules software is often sold as AI.
Exam cue: classify AI by where its logic comes from, and prove it with records of how the system was built, not with labels.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.1 (Tasks and methods the AI system supports are defined)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.1 Kinds of AI Systems (rules engines are not machine learning; classify before you audit). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA pilot, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test, standards audit, concept review).

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Model performance and purpose
questions.question: A food processor's model that flags contaminated batches reports 97% accuracy, but only 3% of batches in its test data were contaminated. What should the IS auditor be MOST concerned about?

options.A: The test data is too small because so few batches were contaminated
options.B: The accuracy figure was produced by the processor's own data team
options.C: The model needs monthly retraining to keep its accuracy current
options.D: The same 97% would result from flagging no batch at all

questions.key_concept: With rare events, high accuracy can hide a model that misses the cases that matter; fitness depends on purpose-relevant error rates.
questions.pre_read: Note any percentages in the stem and ask what a model would score by always predicting the most common outcome.
questions.correct_explanation: With only 3% of batches contaminated, a model that flagged no batch at all would still score 97%. The headline figure therefore cannot show whether the model finds contaminated batches, the one outcome the processor needs. Who produced the figure, option B, is the runner-up: independence matters, but an independently reproduced 97% would be just as misleading for this purpose.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because rare events feel like thin data. But the issue is imbalance, not size; even a large test set with 3% contaminated batches lets accuracy mislead.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because self-reported results are weaker evidence. But the deeper problem is the metric itself; reproducing 97% independently would not show the model finds contaminated batches.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because models can drift. But nothing in the stem shows change over time, and retraining on a fixed schedule does not fix a misleading metric.

tips: Eliminate: A treats imbalance as a sample-size problem, and C prescribes retraining when the stem shows no drift, just a misleading metric.
Final two: D beats B because a misleading metric stays misleading whoever reproduces it; fitness is judged on the errors that matter, here missed contaminated batches.
Exam cue: when the event a model hunts for is rare, distrust overall accuracy and ask how many real cases it catches.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.2 (Potential costs of AI errors examined against risk tolerance)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.2 How Models Learn and Where They Fail (one headline metric can mislead; fitness depends on the errors that matter). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA pilot, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test, standards audit, concept review).

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Requirements and sourcing
questions.question: A university's project charter for a generative AI tutor names the vendor and the model but says nothing about what the tutor must achieve. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the academic owner define the tutor's intended purpose and limits
options.B: Have IT confirm the vendor's model fits the enterprise architecture
options.C: Have the vendor supply accuracy results from several comparable universities
options.D: Have the project team pilot the tutor with volunteer students

questions.key_concept: Business purpose, limits and acceptance criteria come before model, vendor or architecture choices for an AI system.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the project has already decided and what it has skipped, then ask which decision every later step depends on.
questions.correct_explanation: Requirements come before technology. Until the academic owner states what the tutor is for, which uses are out of bounds and how success is judged, nobody can test whether the chosen model fits. Architecture review, option B, is the runner-up: it is a real requirement, but fit can only be judged against a stated purpose, so it follows the business requirement.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because enterprise architecture fit is a genuine AI requirement. But the review needs a stated purpose and limits to assess against, so it comes second.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because evidence from similar customers sounds reassuring. But vendor results are inputs, not assurance, and they cannot show fit to a purpose nobody has defined.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because pilots reduce risk. But a pilot without stated outcomes has nothing to measure, so it cannot show whether the tutor works.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on vendor results, which are inputs rather than assurance, and D pilots without success criteria, so the pilot has nothing to measure.
Final two: A beats B because architecture fit is judged against the business requirement; the owner's purpose and limits must exist before IT can assess fit.
Exam cue: when a project names a model or vendor before a purpose, recommend that the business owner define purpose, limits and acceptance criteria first.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.1 (Intended purposes, context and laws documented); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.6 (System requirements elicited from relevant AI actors)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.3 Business Requirements and Architecture Fit (requirements before technology; architecture fit follows purpose). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA pilot, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Agentic AI considerations
questions.question: A travel company wants its customer-service assistant to rebook flights and issue refunds by itself, rather than just answer questions. Which consideration should the IS auditor raise as MOST important?

options.A: Whether the underlying language model scores well on public benchmarks
options.B: Whether customers are told that they are dealing with an AI assistant
options.C: Whether human approval is required above set payment and change limits
options.D: Whether a sample of the assistant's answers is checked for accuracy monthly

questions.key_concept: Agentic AI acts through tools and systems, so its key requirement is bounded authority with human approval above set limits.
questions.pre_read: Notice what new power the system gains in the stem, and ask what could go wrong once it can act rather than advise.
questions.correct_explanation: Moving from answering to acting makes this agentic AI: it now spends money and changes bookings through other systems. The most important control is a defined boundary on what it may do alone and when a person must approve. Disclosure to customers, option B, is the runner-up: transparency matters, but it does not stop a wrong refund or booking.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because strong benchmarks suggest a capable model. But public benchmarks say nothing about safe actions inside this company's booking and payment systems.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because people should know when AI serves them. But disclosure already mattered when it only answered questions; it does not limit refunds or bookings.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because output review is a common AI control. But checking answers misses the new risk: actions taken on bookings and payments.

tips: Eliminate: A rests on public benchmarks, which do not show safe behavior in this setting, and D reviews answers when the new risk lies in actions.
Final two: C beats B because once AI can act on money and records, limits and human approval prevent harm; disclosure informs customers but prevents nothing.
Exam cue: when an AI system gains the power to act, look first for limits on its actions and a person who approves or can stop them.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.5 (Processes for human oversight defined and assessed); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 2.4 (Mechanisms and responsibilities to supersede, disengage or deactivate AI)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.3 Business Requirements and Architecture Fit (agentic designs need limits on what the system may do without a person). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA pilot, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test, standards audit, concept review).

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Accountability for AI decisions
questions.question: A hospital network uses a vendor's AI model to schedule operating rooms. Who should the IS auditor expect to hold PRIMARY accountability for the schedules the model produces?

options.A: The vendor that built, trained and hosts the scheduling model
options.B: The data science team that integrated and now monitors the model
options.C: The named business owner of surgical scheduling at the hospital
options.D: The AI governance committee that approved the model for use

questions.key_concept: Every model and AI-supported decision needs a named business owner; vendors, builders and committees cannot hold that accountability.
questions.pre_read: Separate who builds, who approves and who uses the output, then ask which of them answers for each result.
questions.correct_explanation: Every AI-supported decision needs a named human owner in the business that uses it. The owner of surgical scheduling answers for the schedules, decides on overrides and accepts the model's risks within appetite. The governance committee, option D, is the runner-up: it approves high-impact use and sets standards, but a committee approving a use case does not own each decision the model makes.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the vendor knows the model best. But accountability cannot be outsourced; the hospital uses the schedules and answers to patients and regulators.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the team understands the model technically. But building and monitoring a model does not make a team the owner of business decisions.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the committee approved the model. But collective approval of a use case is oversight, not ownership of each schedule the model produces.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes a vendor can carry accountability, which stays with the user, and B treats technical builders as owners of business decisions.
Final two: C beats D because a committee approves and oversees, while one named business owner answers for each AI-supported decision day to day.
Exam cue: for who is accountable for AI output, look for a named owner in the business that uses it, never the model, vendor or builders.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 2.1 (Roles, responsibilities and lines of communication documented); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (Roles, responsibilities and authorities established)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.2 Ownership, Roles and the AI Governance Committee (a named business owner for every model and AI decision; committees approve, owners answer). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA pilot, 30 Oct 2026. Cross-domain review fixes 30 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. AI policy risk tiers
questions.question: A logistics firm's board-approved AI policy sends every AI use through one light approval step, from a meeting-notes summarizer to a model that screens job applicants. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the policy owner tier approval steps by each AI use's impact
options.B: Have the AI governance committee approve every AI use
options.C: Have HR suspend applicant screening until the policy is revised
options.D: Have IT review each AI tool's security before approval

questions.key_concept: An AI policy scales approval and oversight to each use's risk tier, set by impact on people and the business.
questions.pre_read: Compare what could go wrong with each AI use the policy treats the same way.
questions.correct_explanation: An AI policy should scale its controls to each use's impact: a tool summarizing internal notes and a model screening job applicants carry very different risk to people. Risk tiers let low-impact uses move quickly and send high-impact ones to deeper review. Committee approval of every use, option B, is the runner-up: it adds rigor, but treating all uses alike swamps the committee and still ignores impact.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because committee review adds rigor. But approving every use alike wastes effort on trivial tools and still ignores which uses can harm people.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because screening people is high risk. But suspending one use leaves the flat policy in place for every other high-impact use, and suspension is management's call.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because security review is familiar. But security is one dimension; the gap is that approval ignores harm to people from AI decisions.

tips: Eliminate: C suspends one use and leaves the flat policy unfixed, and D reduces AI approval to a security check.
Final two: A beats B because approval effort should follow each use's impact; sending everything to the committee is uniform, not risk-based.
Exam cue: when an AI policy treats every use alike, recommend risk tiers that scale approval and review to impact on people and the business.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.3 (Level of risk management activity set by risk tolerance); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.4 (Risk management process established through transparent policies and controls)

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Policy duties for staff
questions.question: A telecom company's AI policy requires staff to check generative AI drafts for invented facts, but training covers only tool use, and most drafts go out unedited. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the vendor add a policy reminder banner to every draft
options.B: Have team leaders sample sent replies monthly for unchecked drafts
options.C: Have IT limit the tool to staff who finished the tool training
options.D: Have the policy owner add the checking duty to the training

questions.key_concept: Awareness and training must teach the specific duties the AI policy imposes; detective sampling is a backstop, not the fix.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the policy requires with what people are taught, and ask where the gap starts.
questions.correct_explanation: Awareness must match the policy. Staff must catch invented facts but were never taught how, and drafts going out unedited suggest they trust fluent AI output. Adding the checking duty to training fixes the cause. Sampling sent replies, option B, is the runner-up: it is a useful detective control, but it finds unchecked drafts only after customers have received them.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a reminder is cheap and visible. But a banner does not teach staff how to spot invented facts, and people soon click past it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because monitoring shows whether the policy works. But it detects failures after customers are affected and leaves the training gap that causes them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it restricts the tool to trained users. But tool training teaches tool skill, not the checking duty the policy requires.

tips: Eliminate: A adds a reminder banner, which does not teach how to spot invented facts, and C limits use to tool-trained staff, though tool training is the gap.
Final two: D beats B because aligning training with the policy prevents unchecked drafts at the source; sampling sent replies detects them afterward.
Exam cue: when staff accept AI output unedited and training skips the policy's duty, recommend that the policy owner align training with that duty.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 2.2 (AI risk management training for personnel and partners); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-2 (Literacy Training and Awareness)

Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA pilot, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test, standards audit, concept review).

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Workforce impact
questions.question: A car rental company's AI assistant will resolve most billing calls; agents, whose training is unchanged, will take escalations and review a sample of its answers. Which risk should the IS auditor consider GREATEST?

options.A: Customers may prefer human agents and complain about the change
options.B: Agents may lack the skills for complex cases and checking AI output
options.C: The assistant may give inconsistent answers to identical billing questions
options.D: License costs may not be recovered within the first year

questions.key_concept: AI changes roles: remaining staff take harder cases and oversee AI output, so workforce plans must reskill them before go-live.
questions.pre_read: Ask how each group's job changes after the AI goes live, and whether anything in the stem prepares them for it.
questions.correct_explanation: Agents now take the hardest calls and are the human check on the assistant's answers, yet their training is unchanged, so both complex cases and AI errors may be mishandled. Inconsistent answers, option C, is the runner-up: a real generative AI risk, but the agents' sample review is the control meant to catch it, and untrained reviewers weaken that control.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because customer reaction matters. But preference and complaints are a change-management issue, smaller than staff unprepared for the work that remains.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because generative output can vary. But the agents' sample review is the control for that risk, and it is only as good as their training.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because AI investments must pay back. But cost recovery is a value question, not the main risk created by unchanged training.

tips: Eliminate: A is a change-management concern about customer preference, and D is a value question about cost recovery; neither follows from the unchanged training.
Final two: B beats C because the agents' review is the control that would catch inconsistent answers; untrained reviewers are the root cause that weakens it.
Exam cue: when AI takes over routine work, ask whether the people left behind were trained for the harder work and oversight they now carry.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Appetite and tolerance
questions.question: A pharmaceutical company is drafting its first AI risk appetite statement. Which party should the IS auditor expect to hold PRIMARY responsibility for approving it?

options.A: The lead data scientist, who knows each model's error rates
options.B: The internal audit function, which assesses AI risk independently
options.C: The AI governance committee, which reviews each AI use case
options.D: The board of directors, on senior management's recommendation

questions.key_concept: The board approves AI risk appetite; management and owners set tolerances and criteria within it, and the auditor assesses them.
questions.pre_read: Separate who sets limits, who applies them and who assesses them before choosing a party.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk appetite expresses how much AI risk the organization will take to pursue its goals, so the board approves it, usually on management's proposal. Management then sets tolerances within it, and committees and owners apply them. The AI governance committee, option C, is the runner-up: it applies appetite to use cases and may draft the statement, but it works within the appetite rather than approving it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because data scientists know the models' error rates. But error limits express how much harm the company accepts; the board sets appetite.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because internal audit understands AI risk. But setting appetite is a governance decision; the auditor assesses it and must stay independent of it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the committee governs AI day to day. But it applies the appetite to each use case; the board approves the appetite itself.

tips: Eliminate: A has a data scientist setting limits that express how much harm the company accepts, and B puts the independent auditor in a governance decision it must later assess.
Final two: D beats C because the committee works within appetite case by case, while the board approves how much AI risk the organization accepts.
Exam cue: the board approves risk appetite; management sets tolerances within it, owners apply them, and auditors assess them.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Board reporting on AI risk
questions.question: A traffic authority's senior management set a tolerance for fines wrongly issued by its AI camera model, yet monthly reports show just the number of fines issued. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add officer review of every fine before drivers are notified
options.B: Report the wrongful-fine rate with thresholds that trigger escalation
options.C: Retrain the camera model each quarter to keep decisions current
options.D: Send the fine volume report to the board weekly, not monthly

questions.key_concept: AI tolerances need key risk indicators that measure harm against the limit; activity volumes are not risk indicators.
questions.pre_read: Match what management limited with what the reports actually measure, and look for the missing link.
questions.correct_explanation: Management set a tolerance, but nobody measures against it: the number of fines shows activity, not harm. A key risk indicator that tracks the wrongful-fine rate against the tolerance, with escalation thresholds, tells management and the board when to act. Officer review of every fine, option A, is the runner-up: it is a possible response, but choosing it before anyone knows the error rate is premature, and the owner decides responses.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because human review catches wrong fines. But it is a costly response chosen before the error rate is known, and it still gives management no measure.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because retraining can improve decisions. But nothing shows the model is failing, and a fixed schedule does not create the missing measure.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because faster reporting seems more vigilant. But reporting the wrong metric more often still says nothing about wrongly issued fines.

tips: Eliminate: C retrains without evidence of failure and adds no measure, and D speeds up a volume report, which tracks activity rather than harm.
Final two: B beats A because the gap is measurement against tolerance; a key risk indicator shows whether action is needed, and the owner then chooses the response.
Exam cue: when a tolerance exists but reports show volumes, recommend a key risk indicator measured against that tolerance with an escalation path.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Third-party AI risk
questions.question: A transit agency will license a vendor's bus-maintenance prediction model, which the vendor updates several times a year. Which contract term should the IS auditor consider MOST important for managing the AI risk?

options.A: Notice and a right to test before the vendor changes the model
options.B: A guaranteed accuracy level for predictions, backed by service credits
options.C: Vendor liability for every decision the agency makes using the model
options.D: A right to audit physical security at the vendor's data centers

questions.key_concept: Third-party AI contracts should give notice and testing rights over model changes; accountability and assurance cannot be bought with guarantees.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the vendor can change after signing without the buyer knowing, and which term would expose that.
questions.correct_explanation: The vendor updates the model several times a year, and an update the agency has not tested can make predictions unsafe overnight. Notice and the right to test changes on the agency's own data keep the agency in control of what it relies on. The accuracy guarantee, option B, is the runner-up: credits compensate after failures, and an overall accuracy level cannot show each update still works on the agency's fleet.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it puts a number in the contract. But credits pay after failures rather than preventing unsafe predictions, and one overall level cannot show each update suits this fleet.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it seems to shift risk. But accountability for decisions stays with the agency that relies on the model; contracts cannot transfer it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because audit rights are standard. But data center security says nothing about whether the model's predictions stay valid after changes.

tips: Eliminate: C tries to transfer accountability, which stays with the agency, and D audits the vendor's facilities, which do not show how the model behaves.
Final two: A beats B because testing each update before use prevents unvalidated predictions; an accuracy guarantee compensates afterward and cannot show an update suits this fleet.
Exam cue: for third-party AI, value contract rights to see and test model changes over promises that only compensate after a failure.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Rating AI risk
questions.question: A housing authority's risk register rates a model flagging tenants for eviction review as low risk, citing secure hosting and no outages. Which question should the IS auditor raise as MOST significant?

options.A: Whether the hosting security evidence was independently verified
options.B: Whether the hosting contract sets a recovery time for tenant cases
options.C: Whether the rating weighs the harm wrong flags cause tenants
options.D: Whether the register records which algorithm the model uses

questions.key_concept: AI risk ratings must weigh harm to affected people from wrong outputs, not only security and availability of the system.
questions.pre_read: Read the reason given for the rating and ask whether it measures the harm this model's errors could cause.
questions.correct_explanation: The rating rests on security and availability, yet the model's main risk is a wrong flag pushing a tenant toward eviction. AI risk assessment must weigh the likelihood and impact of harm to affected people, not only to systems. Unverified security evidence, option A, is the runner-up: verifying it would improve the evidence, but a confirmed secure, stable model can still harm many tenants.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because unverified evidence is weak. But even independently confirmed security would not change the rating's real gap: harm to tenants from wrong flags.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because recovery targets are a standard continuity control. But availability is not the model's main risk; wrong flags harm tenants even when it runs perfectly.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because documentation supports review. But naming the algorithm adds detail without changing the rating; impact on people drives AI risk.

tips: Eliminate: B adds another availability control when availability is not the main risk, and D records algorithm detail, which does not change the rating.
Final two: C beats A because better evidence for security still leaves the rating blind to harm; AI risk ratings must weigh impact on affected people.
Exam cue: when an AI risk rating cites security or uptime, ask who is harmed when the model is wrong, and how badly.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Scraped training data
questions.question: A fitness app company plans to train a model on public forum posts scraped from the web, including users' health details. What should the IS auditor consider the PRIMARY privacy concern?

options.A: Whether the company may lawfully use this personal data for training
options.B: Whether the scraped posts are accurate enough to train a good model
options.C: Whether forum operators can detect and block the company's scraping tool
options.D: Whether the posts are stored on encrypted servers once collected

questions.key_concept: Public availability does not by itself grant the right to train on personal data; permitted use comes before security controls.
questions.pre_read: Separate whether the data may be used from how well it is protected, and ask which question comes first.
questions.correct_explanation: Personal health details are sensitive, and posting them publicly does not by itself give anyone the right to reuse them for model training. The first privacy question is whether a legal basis, consent or permitted purpose covers this new use. Encrypted storage, option D, is the runner-up: it protects the data from outsiders, but it cannot make an unpermitted use lawful.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because data quality shapes the model. But accuracy is a data-quality question; the privacy question is whether the data may be used for training.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because scraping can breach site terms. But whether operators can block the tool is a technical matter, not the privacy concern for users' health details.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because security protects personal data. But encryption guards against outsiders; it does not decide whether training on this data is permitted.

tips: Eliminate: B is a data-quality question rather than a privacy one, and C concerns the scraping technique, not the rights of people whose health details appear.
Final two: A beats D because security protects data the company may hold, while privacy first asks whether this use of personal data is permitted.
Exam cue: publicly visible personal data is not free to use for training; ask about the right to use it before how it is protected.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Erasure requests
questions.question: A language-learning app deletes a former user's records after an erasure request, but the user's essays were used to fine-tune its writing-feedback model. What should the IS auditor be MOST concerned about?

options.A: The deletion was not confirmed to the former user in writing
options.B: Backup copies of the essays may remain for ninety days
options.C: The trained model may still reproduce parts of the essays
options.D: The model's accuracy may fall once the essays are deleted

questions.key_concept: Trained and fine-tuned models can memorize training data, so erasure must consider affected models, not only source records.
questions.pre_read: Trace where the user's data went after collection, including anything built from it, before judging the deletion.
questions.correct_explanation: Fine-tuning can make a model memorize distinctive training text and reproduce it later, so deleting the source records may leave the user's essays inside the model. The erasure process must consider affected models. Backups, option B, is the runner-up: they are a known deletion gap, but they expire on a schedule, while a deployed model keeps serving what it learned with no expiry.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because confirmation is part of handling requests. But it is a process step; the essays may still exist inside the model.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because backups are a classic deletion gap. But they expire on schedule and stay offline, while the deployed model can keep exposing the essays.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because data loss can affect models. But deleting records does not change an already trained model, which is exactly why the essays may persist.

tips: Eliminate: A is a procedural step that leaves the data in place, and D assumes deleting records changes a trained model, which it does not.
Final two: C beats B because backups expire offline on schedule, while a deployed model can keep reproducing memorized text to users indefinitely.
Exam cue: when personal data used for training is erased, ask what the trained model still holds before checking backups and paperwork.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Data feeds for models
questions.question: A dairy cooperative retrains its milk-supply forecasting model weekly on six data feeds, but no one can say who owns two of the feeds or where they originate. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Drop the two feeds and retrain the model on the other four
options.B: Assign owners and trace both feeds' lineage to each model version
options.C: Run data-quality checks on the two feeds before each retraining
options.D: Encrypt the two feeds in transit from their source systems

questions.key_concept: AI data governance starts with a data owner and documented lineage; quality controls and security build on that foundation.
questions.pre_read: Find what nobody in the stem can answer about the data, and ask who would normally be responsible for answering it.
questions.correct_explanation: Without an owner, nobody can approve the feeds' use, vouch for their quality or answer for errors, and without lineage to each model version nobody can tell which weekly retrain absorbed a bad feed. Ownership and lineage come first. Data-quality checks, option C, are the runner-up: they are needed, but someone must own the rules, act on failures and confirm the data may be used.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because removing doubtful data seems safe. But retraining before diagnosis may weaken forecasts, and the feeds may be valid once owned and traced.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because quality checks catch bad data before retraining. But with no owner, nobody sets the rules, fixes failures or confirms the data may be used.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because protecting data in transit is good practice. But encryption secures delivery; it says nothing about who owns the feeds or where they originate.

tips: Eliminate: A retrains before the cause is known, which can weaken forecasts, and D secures transmission, which does not establish ownership or origin.
Final two: B beats C because quality checks need an owner to set rules and act on failures; ownership and lineage are the foundation data governance builds on.
Exam cue: when data feeding a retrained model has no owner or known origin, recommend owners and lineage to model versions before adding technical checks.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Combining training data
questions.question: A research nonprofit that de-identified patient records two years ago to train a model now plans to add a partner's location data to the training set. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Encrypt the combined training set before the model is retrained
options.B: Obtain the partner's written assurance that its data is accurate
options.C: Retrain the model and compare its accuracy with the current one
options.D: Update the privacy impact assessment for re-identification risk

questions.key_concept: De-identification can fail when datasets are combined, so privacy impact assessments must be updated before new sources join training data.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the new data source makes possible when joined to the old one, and who could exploit it.
questions.correct_explanation: Data de-identified once can become identifiable when combined with new sources; location data is a classic key for linking records back to people. Before the data is combined, the privacy impact assessment must be updated for this new re-identification risk. Encryption, option A, is the runner-up: it protects the set from outsiders, but authorized users and the model's outputs could still re-identify patients.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because encryption protects sensitive data. But it guards against outsiders; it does not stop people with access, or model outputs, linking records back to patients.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because partner data quality matters. But accuracy assurance addresses quality, not the privacy risk that combining datasets creates.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it tests the change. But retraining first combines the data before the privacy risk is assessed, and accuracy says nothing about re-identification.

tips: Eliminate: B addresses the partner's data quality rather than privacy, and C combines and retrains before anyone has assessed the new risk.
Final two: D beats A because combining datasets can re-identify patients even for authorized users; the impact assessment must come before any protective control is chosen.
Exam cue: de-identification is not permanent; when new data sources are added, expect the privacy impact assessment to be updated first.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Status of AI frameworks
questions.question: A board member says US law requires the company to follow the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. How should the IS auditor BEST treat the framework when setting audit criteria?

options.A: As binding law, so every gap is reported as noncompliance
options.B: As voluntary guidance, usable as criteria if it is suitable
options.C: As unsuitable for criteria until a law makes it mandatory
options.D: As a certification scheme proving the company's AI is trustworthy

questions.key_concept: The NIST AI RMF is voluntary guidance, not law; the auditor may still select it as audit criteria when it is suitable.
questions.pre_read: Ask what kind of document the framework is: law, standard or guidance, and who would make it binding.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST publishes the AI RMF as voluntary guidance, so the framework itself imposes no legal duty on the company. The auditor selects audit criteria for suitability, and a recognized voluntary framework often qualifies; the auditor then communicates the chosen criteria to management. Treating it as unsuitable until mandated, option C, is the runner-up: it avoids overstating duties, but criteria must be suitable, not legally required.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because NIST is a US federal agency. But it publishes this framework as voluntary guidance; legal duties come from laws and contracts.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it avoids treating guidance as law. But criteria need to be suitable, not mandated; recognized voluntary frameworks often serve well.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because frameworks are often linked with certificates. But the AI RMF has no certification scheme, and no certificate alone proves AI trustworthy.

tips: Eliminate: A treats the framework as law, though NIST publishes it as voluntary, and D invents a certification scheme the framework does not have.
Final two: B beats C because the auditor selects criteria for suitability, not legal force; a recognized voluntary framework is often suitable.
Exam cue: separate what a source is (law, voluntary framework, certifiable standard) from whether the auditor can select it as suitable audit criteria.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. AI ethics statements
questions.question: A pension fund's AI ethics statement says its member-service models must be fair and explainable, but nothing defines how either quality will be judged. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Publish the ethics statement on the fund's website for members
options.B: Have model developers sign that their models meet the statement
options.C: Engage an external firm to certify the models as ethical
options.D: Have model owners set metrics and thresholds for each principle

questions.key_concept: Trustworthy-AI principles must become measurable criteria with owners and thresholds before they can be tested or certified.
questions.pre_read: Ask what an independent tester would need in hand before they could say whether a model is fair.
questions.correct_explanation: A principle cannot be audited until someone defines it for the use: a metric, a threshold, a test method and an owner. Measurable criteria turn fair and explainable into tests that independent reviewers can run. External certification, option C, is the runner-up: independent review is valuable, but without agreed criteria the firm has nothing to certify against.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because transparency is a trustworthy-AI value. But publishing an untestable statement adds visibility, not criteria anyone can test.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it creates a record. But builders attesting to their own work is not independent evidence, and the statement still has no measure.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because external review is independent. But a firm needs defined criteria to test against; certifying undefined principles gives false comfort.

tips: Eliminate: A publicizes a statement that still cannot be tested, and B relies on the builders' self-attestation, which is not independent evidence.
Final two: D beats C because criteria must exist before anyone can test against them; certifying undefined principles proves nothing about fairness or explainability.
Exam cue: when principles have no measures, recommend that owners define metrics, thresholds and test methods before any testing or certification.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. New AI laws
questions.question: An airline learns that a new AI law in one of its markets treats its crew-rostering model as high risk. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Switch off the model in that market until the law is clarified
options.B: Buy a compliance tool that scans each model against AI regulations
options.C: Have legal counsel and the model owner map each duty to controls
options.D: Apply the new law's requirements to every AI system worldwide

questions.key_concept: New AI obligations are mapped to controls, owners and evidence first; strategy and tooling choices follow the mapping.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the organization must know about the new duties before any response can be judged adequate.
questions.correct_explanation: The first step is to know exactly which duties apply to this model and whether controls already meet them. Mapping each obligation to a control, an owner and evidence shows the gaps to close. Applying the law everywhere, option D, is the runner-up: a global baseline can be a sound strategy, but it is a later management choice that still needs the mapping first.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it avoids exposure. But a high-risk label usually adds duties rather than banning use, and switching off a working model is management's decision.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because tools track regulations. But a tool cannot decide applicability, assign owners or produce evidence; governance comes before tooling.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because one standard is simpler. But extending duties worldwide is a strategy choice for management, and it still requires knowing the duties first.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a high-risk label as a ban, when such laws mostly add duties, and B buys tooling before anyone has decided which duties apply.
Final two: C beats D because a worldwide rollout still depends on knowing each duty and its control gap; mapping comes first and informs management's strategy.
Exam cue: when a new AI law applies, map each obligation to a control, owner and evidence before choosing tools or strategies.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. High-impact public services
questions.question: A social services agency's model, which passed a legal compliance review, ranks which family support cases get urgent visits, but caseworkers cannot explain its rankings. Which concern should the IS auditor consider GREATEST?

options.A: Staff cannot meaningfully question or override the model's priorities
options.B: The legal review may not cover every jurisdiction the agency serves
options.C: The model's source code may not be available for inspection
options.D: The agency may face higher costs if the law later changes

questions.key_concept: High-impact AI needs explainability sufficient for real human oversight and appeal; legal compliance alone does not provide it.
questions.pre_read: Ask who must act on the model's output and what they need to understand before they can challenge it.
questions.correct_explanation: Rankings that decide which families get urgent help are high impact, and the people overseeing them must understand them well enough to question and override them. If caseworkers cannot explain the rankings, oversight becomes a rubber stamp and families have no meaningful appeal. Jurisdiction coverage, option B, is the runner-up: it is a fair question, but full legal compliance would still leave the oversight gap.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because compliance gaps carry penalties. But even complete legal compliance would not let caseworkers understand or challenge rankings that affect families.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because code review seems to reveal logic. But a learned model's behavior lies in its training and parameters; source code alone rarely explains a ranking.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because changing laws affect budgets. But cost is a planning concern, not the main risk from rankings nobody can explain.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes source code explains a learned model, which rarely holds, and D is a budget concern rather than a risk to the families affected.
Final two: A beats B because passing a legal review does not make oversight real; caseworkers who cannot explain rankings cannot override them or support appeals.
Exam cue: for high-impact AI, legal compliance is a floor; check that the people overseeing it can understand, override and stop it.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Generative AI answers
questions.question: A labor ministry's staff believe its generative AI chatbot looks up current wage rules when workers ask questions, but it is connected to no document source. Which risk should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: Workers may not be told that they are chatting with an AI
options.B: The wage-rules database may be unavailable during busy periods
options.C: Workers may get confident answers matching no wage rule in force
options.D: The chatbot may word the same answer differently each time

questions.key_concept: Generative AI predicts plausible text rather than looking facts up, so answers not grounded in checked sources can be confidently wrong.
questions.pre_read: Ask how this kind of AI produces an answer, and compare that with what the staff believe it does.
questions.correct_explanation: A generative model with no document source does not look rules up; it predicts plausible text from patterns in its training data, so answers can be outdated or invented. Workers may act on confident but wrong wage answers. Disclosure, option A, is the runner-up: workers should know they are using AI, but knowing does not make a wrong wage rule right.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because workers should know they are using AI. But disclosure does not stop the chatbot stating wage rules that do not exist.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because lookups depend on a database. But this chatbot is connected to no source; it generates answers, so database availability is not the risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because varied wording looks unreliable. But different phrasing of a correct rule harms no one; the risk is content that is wrong.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes a database lookup the chatbot never makes, and D worries about wording, which harms no one when the content is right.
Final two: C beats A because generative AI can state invented or outdated rules with confidence; disclosure informs workers but does not make answers correct.
Exam cue: a generative model predicts plausible text; unless it is grounded in checked sources, expect confident errors, not lookups.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Systems combining two kinds of AI
questions.question: A Jamaican apprenticeship program's predictive model scores applicants, and a generative model then writes each rejection letter's reasons from the application. Which concern should the IS auditor consider GREATEST?

options.A: The stated reasons may not reflect what actually drove each score
options.B: Drafted reasons holding personal data may be kept longer than needed
options.C: The scoring model may be less accurate for some groups of applicants
options.D: The two models may come from vendors with different contract terms

questions.key_concept: A generative model writes plausible text, so reasons it drafts may not match what a separate predictive model actually used to score.
questions.pre_read: Notice how many AI systems the stem describes, and what each one does with the applicant's file.
questions.correct_explanation: The score comes from the predictive model, but the reasons come from a generative model reading the application, which produces plausible text rather than tracing the score's drivers. Applicants may get reasons that are fluent but false, which undermines any appeal. Unequal accuracy across groups, option C, is the runner-up: it deserves testing, but nothing here points to it, while the letter design builds in the mismatch.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because drafted reasons hold personal data. But over-retention is a records-management risk, smaller than telling applicants reasons that did not drive their rejection.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because scoring models can treat groups unequally. But nothing here suggests it, while the letter design itself separates the stated reasons from the score.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because two suppliers mean two contracts. But contract terms are a third-party question; they do not affect whether letters state the true reasons.

tips: Eliminate: D is a supplier-terms question, and B is a records-retention point; neither affects whether applicants are told the true reasons.
Final two: A beats C because the design lets a generative model write plausible reasons the score never used; group accuracy deserves testing but has no support here.
Exam cue: when one AI system decides and another explains, check that the explanation is built from the decision's real drivers.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Ranking reader comments
questions.question: A news publisher's model ranks comments so the most useful appear first; trained on reply counts, it predicts them with 91% accuracy on held-out comments. What should the IS auditor be MOST concerned about?

options.A: Readers may not know that a model ranks the comments they see
options.B: The 91% accuracy may fall as news topics shift over time
options.C: The training set may hold too few months of past comments
options.D: The training label may not match the ranking's business goal

questions.key_concept: A model learns the label it is trained on; a proxy label can make it accurate at the wrong thing.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the business wants the model to do with what it was actually trained to predict.
questions.correct_explanation: A model optimizes the label people give it. Reply counts are only a proxy for usefulness, and heated comments often draw the most replies, so 91% accuracy shows the model is good at the wrong thing. Drift, option B, is the runner-up: topics do shift and accuracy needs monitoring, but monitoring would only keep the model good at predicting replies, not usefulness.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because transparency matters. But telling readers a model ranks comments does not fix a model trained toward the wrong goal.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because models drift as topics change. But monitoring drift would only keep the model good at predicting replies, not at finding useful comments.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because models learn from data. But more months of reply counts would only teach the model the wrong goal more firmly.

tips: Eliminate: A is a disclosure point that leaves the wrong objective in place, and C worries about data volume, though more reply data only teaches the wrong goal more firmly.
Final two: D beats B because drift monitoring keeps a model good at its learned target; the reply-count label itself is the root problem.
Exam cue: a high accuracy score shows a model predicts its label well; check that label against the business goal before trusting the score.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Alert thresholds
questions.question: A Canadian wildfire agency's data team set its ignition-alert model's cut-off score to maximize overall accuracy, which treats a missed fire and a false alarm alike. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the data team lower the cut-off until no fire is missed
options.B: Have the model owner set the cut-off from each error's cost
options.C: Have the model owner order retraining on more fire seasons
options.D: Have an independent team revalidate the model's overall accuracy

questions.key_concept: Where to set a model's cut-off is a business choice about error costs, made by the model owner, not a technical default like accuracy.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each kind of model error costs here, and who should decide how much of each is acceptable.
questions.correct_explanation: A cut-off decides how many missed fires the agency trades for false alarms, and a missed fire usually costs far more. That trade-off is a business decision for the model owner, within the agency's tolerances, not a default chosen to maximize accuracy. Pushing misses to zero, option A, is the runner-up: it weighs the costlier error, but it ignores the cost of false alarms and leaves the builders deciding.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because missed fires are costly. But pushing misses toward zero floods crews with false alarms, and the data team would still be making the owner's trade-off.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because more data often improves models. But retraining leaves the cut-off choice unchanged; how errors are weighed is a decision, not a data gap.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because independent checks add assurance. But revalidating overall accuracy confirms the same metric; it does not weigh a missed fire against a false alarm.

tips: Eliminate: C adds data when the issue is how errors are weighed, and D revalidates overall accuracy, the same metric that treats both errors alike.
Final two: B beats A because the owner must weigh both error costs; chasing zero misses floods crews with false alarms, and the data team would still be deciding.
Exam cue: a model's threshold is a business decision on error costs, set by the owner within tolerance, never a technical default.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Choosing an approach
questions.question: A Zambian land registry plans a machine-learning model to check whether title applications are complete, though completeness is defined by a published checklist of required fields. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the business owner assess whether a rules engine meets the need
options.B: Have the business owner set accuracy targets before the model is trained
options.C: Have the team gather five years of past applications for training
options.D: Have a vendor demonstrate its model on sample applications

questions.key_concept: Requirements come before technology: when fixed, published rules define a task, a rules-based check may meet the need without machine learning's added risks.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the task is defined by rules people already wrote, and what learning from data would add.
questions.correct_explanation: Completeness here is defined by a published checklist, so the task is a fixed rule set. A learned model would add training data, error rates, drift and explainability work for no stated gain. The business owner should first weigh a rules-based check against the requirement. Setting accuracy targets, option B, is the runner-up: it is sound requirement practice, but it assumes machine learning is the answer.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because acceptance criteria should come before building. But targets for a model assume a model is needed; fixed published rules may not need one.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because models need training data. But gathering data commits to machine learning before anyone asks whether the checklist already defines the task.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a demonstration shows what a product can do. But vendor demonstrations are inputs, and they skip whether the registry needs a model.

tips: Eliminate: C gathers training data before asking whether a model is needed, and D relies on a vendor demonstration, which is an input, not a requirement.
Final two: A beats B because accuracy targets assume machine learning; a task defined by published rules may be better met by a rules-based check.
Exam cue: start from the requirement, not the technology; when written rules fully define a task, expect non-AI options to be weighed first.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Architecture review
questions.question: A stadium operator's gate-staffing model was trained on turnstile data refreshed every five minutes, but an architecture review finds production will receive only a nightly export. Which concern should the IS auditor consider MOST important?

options.A: The hosting region may differ from where the operator's other systems run
options.B: Running the model may cost more than the business case assumed
options.C: The model would score day-old data unlike the data it learned from
options.D: The nightly data export may fail without anyone being alerted

questions.key_concept: A model performs as validated only when production feeds it data like its training data; architecture reviews must check that fit.
questions.pre_read: Compare the data the model learned from with the data it will receive in production.
questions.correct_explanation: The model learned patterns from turnstile data a few minutes old; in production it would assign gate staff using data up to a day old, so its predictions would rest on conditions it was never trained or validated on. Export monitoring, option D, is the runner-up: a failed job is a real operational gap, but even a perfect nightly export leaves the mismatch.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because hosting location is part of architecture review. But where the model runs does not change what data it receives or how old that data is.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because architecture review covers running costs. But cost is a value question; a model fed unfamiliar data fails its purpose whatever it costs.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because unmonitored batch jobs fail silently. But a reliable nightly export still gives the model day-old data it was not built for.

tips: Eliminate: A raises hosting location, which does not change the data the model receives, and B raises cost, a value question after whether the model can work.
Final two: C beats D because even a flawless nightly export feeds the model day-old data unlike its training; job monitoring cannot fix the mismatch.
Exam cue: in an architecture review of AI, check that production feeds the model data like the data it was trained and validated on.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. AI features in purchased tools
questions.question: A Malaysian palm-oil producer's AI policy checks tools only at purchase; HR switched off an AI assistant that a vendor update added to its approved HR tool. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the policy owner arrange a risk review of the AI assistant
options.B: Have IT put the HR tool's update through security review
options.C: Have the data team retrain the assistant on company HR data
options.D: Have the policy owner trigger review whenever a tool gains AI

questions.key_concept: AI policy must catch AI that arrives through vendor updates to approved software, not only AI reviewed at purchase or built in-house.
questions.pre_read: Find why the assistant was never reviewed, and ask whether fixing it alone would stop the next one.
questions.correct_explanation: The policy checks AI only at purchase, yet vendors now add AI features to approved software through routine updates, so this assistant arrived unreviewed. HR has already switched it off, so the open risk is the next one. A review trigger whenever a tool gains AI fixes the cause. Reviewing this assistant, option A, is the runner-up: it is needed before reuse, but it fixes one instance while the purchase-only trigger keeps missing the next.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the assistant needs review before HR turns it back on. But that fixes one instance; the purchase-only trigger will miss the next AI feature an update brings.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because updates often get security review. But security review skips AI risks such as wrong outputs, and the purchase-only trigger would still miss the next AI feature.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because company data can improve fit. But retraining a vendor's assistant is a technical fix before any review, and the purchase-only trigger would still miss the next feature.

tips: Eliminate: C retrains the vendor's assistant before anyone has reviewed it, a technical fix ahead of governance, and B uses a security review that skips AI risks such as wrong outputs.
Final two: D beats A because the assistant is already off and reviewing it treats the symptom; a trigger whenever a tool gains AI catches the next one too.
Exam cue: AI now arrives through updates to software already approved. Once the slipped-through instance is contained, the BEST recommendation fixes the policy trigger that let it bypass review.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. AI strategy review
questions.question: A childcare-subsidy agency's draft AI strategy aims to fully automate subsidy decisions within two years; its board's appetite for wrongly refused subsidies is low. What should the IS auditor raise as MOST important?

options.A: The strategy may not name a preferred vendor or model platform
options.B: The strategy may plan more automation than the board would accept
options.C: The accuracy promised to the board may not be validated independently
options.D: Agency staff may resist the change once automation is announced

questions.key_concept: An AI strategy must fit the board's risk appetite, especially when it removes people from high-impact decisions about individuals.
questions.pre_read: Read the strategy's goal against the board's stated appetite, and ask who is harmed if the two conflict.
questions.correct_explanation: Strategy must fit the board's appetite. Fully automating subsidy decisions removes the human review that could catch wrongful refusals, against a low appetite for exactly that harm, so the strategy may promise what the board would not accept. Unvalidated accuracy, option C, is the runner-up: it deserves challenge, but even validated accuracy leaves some wrongful refusals, which full automation would no longer catch.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because strategies lead to platform choices. But naming a vendor first starts from technology; a strategy should start from objectives and appetite.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because AI accuracy claims need independent proof. But even validated accuracy leaves some wrongful refusals, and full automation removes the person who could catch them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because change brings resistance. But staff acceptance is a change-management issue, smaller than a plan whose wrongful refusals may exceed the board's appetite.

tips: Eliminate: A wants a vendor named, which starts from technology rather than objectives, and D is a change-management concern, not a risk to the people seeking subsidies.
Final two: B beats C because even validated accuracy leaves some wrongful refusals, and full automation removes the review that catches them; the plan must fit the board's appetite.
Exam cue: test an AI strategy against the board's appetite and the people affected, especially when it removes humans from high-impact decisions.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Requests to internal audit
questions.question: A stock exchange's AI governance committee asks the head of IS audit to sign off the builders' pre-launch tests of each surveillance model, as the independent check. What is the BEST response?

options.A: Accept the role and disclose it in later audit reports
options.B: Recommend the committee review the builders' test results before launch
options.C: Recommend a validation function separate from the model builders
options.D: Limit the sign-off role to the highest-risk surveillance models

questions.key_concept: Independent model validation belongs to a function separate from the builders; the IS auditor assesses it but never performs or signs it off.
questions.pre_read: Separate who checks models before launch from who later audits that check, and ask what each role must stay free of.
questions.correct_explanation: Validation before launch is a management control: testers independent of the builders check each model, as the NIST AI RMF expects. If IS audit signs off the builders' tests, it would later audit its own work. A separate validation function gives the committee its check and keeps audit independent. Committee review of the builders' results, option B, is the runner-up: it governs uses, but reading builders' own results is not independent testing.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because disclosure seems to cure a conflict. But disclosure does not restore objectivity once audit has approved the work it reviews.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the committee approves high-impact uses. But reading the builders' own results is not validation; testers independent of the builders must check each model.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it limits the role to where risk is highest. But signing off any validation makes audit part of the control it must assess.

tips: Eliminate: D still has audit signing off validations, and A treats disclosure as a cure, though it cannot restore objectivity over work audit approved.
Final two: C beats B because validation needs testers independent of the builders; a committee reading the builders' own results approves uses but does not validate.
Exam cue: when asked to perform or approve an AI control, the IS auditor recommends who should own it and stays free to assess it.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Choosing a model owner
questions.question: An offshore drilling contractor names a junior analyst as owner of the model that sets rig crews' rest breaks, because the analyst watches its dashboard. Which question should the IS auditor consider MOST important?

options.A: Whether the analyst has authority to accept the model's risks
options.B: Whether the analyst helped build or train the model
options.C: Whether the analyst holds a formal data science qualification
options.D: Whether the analyst's ownership is written into the responsibility chart

questions.key_concept: A model owner must have authority to accept its risks, override its decisions and pause it; watching a dashboard is monitoring, not ownership.
questions.pre_read: Ask what an owner must be able to do when the model's output could hurt someone, then compare it with this role.
questions.correct_explanation: Ownership is accountability with authority: the owner accepts the model's risks within appetite, decides on overrides and can pause the model when rest breaks look unsafe. A junior analyst chosen for watching a dashboard is placed to monitor, and may not hold that authority. Whether the role is written down, option D, is the runner-up: documenting it matters, but a written entry would not give the analyst authority.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because builders know the model best. But owners answer for its use and results; building and training are separate roles.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because AI seems to need technical owners. But ownership calls for business authority over decisions; technical skill sits with the data team.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because roles must be written down. But recording the analyst as owner would not give them authority to accept the model's risks.

tips: Eliminate: B confuses building a model with owning its decisions, and C looks for data science skills, though ownership needs business authority, not technical training.
Final two: A beats D because writing the role down would not give a junior analyst authority to accept the model's risks.
Exam cue: a real model owner can accept the risks, override outputs and stop the model; someone who only monitors it is not the owner.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Long reliance on an AI model
questions.question: A weather service's AI nowcasting model has drafted every storm warning for six years, and the continuity plan assumes forecasters will warn manually if it fails. Which risk should the IS auditor consider GREATEST?

options.A: The model may drift as storm patterns shift from its training data
options.B: Forecasters may resist plans to automate more of their warnings
options.C: The continuity plan may lack sign-off from the board
options.D: Forecasters may no longer be able to warn without the model

questions.key_concept: Long reliance on AI erodes the manual skills that fallback plans assume, so workforce plans must keep those skills current.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the continuity plan expects people to do, and whether their recent work has kept them able to do it.
questions.correct_explanation: The continuity plan relies on forecasters warning without the model, but for six years the model has drafted every warning, so manual skills may have faded or never formed in newer staff. If the model fails during a storm, the fallback may not work. Drift, option A, is the runner-up: it is a real AI risk, but nothing here shows it, and a failing model is exactly when the fallback must work.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because models degrade as conditions change. But nothing here shows drift, and if the model did fail, the manual fallback is what must work.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because automation unsettles staff. But resistance is a change-management concern, smaller than a fallback that may fail during a storm.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because plans need approval. But continuity plans are approved by management; board sign-off would not restore forecasters' manual skills.

tips: Eliminate: B is a change-management worry about staff acceptance, and C asks for board sign-off of an operational plan, which management approves.
Final two: D beats A because the plan assumes manual skills that six years of AI drafting may have eroded; drift has no support here.
Exam cue: when AI has done a task for years, ask whether people can still do it by hand before trusting a manual fallback.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Owners accepting residual risk
questions.question: An airport operator's model owners accept residual risk for its baggage-screening models on one overall accuracy figure each, having had only the all-staff AI awareness course. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the data scientists who build the models sign the acceptances
options.B: Have owners take role-based training on judging model risk
options.C: Have IS audit review each acceptance before the owner signs it
options.D: Have owners raise the overall accuracy bar for accepting risk

questions.key_concept: Owners who accept AI risks need role-based training to judge them; one accuracy figure hides error types, drift and validation limits.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a model owner must understand to accept residual risk, and whether a staff-wide course teaches it.
questions.correct_explanation: Accepting residual risk means judging error types, drift and validation limits, which one overall accuracy figure hides. A course built for all staff does not teach that, so owners may accept risks they cannot weigh. Role-based training equips them and keeps accountability with them. A higher accuracy bar, option D, is the runner-up: it looks stricter, but owners would still judge from the one number that hides the risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because builders understand the models. But accepting risk is a business decision; builders signing for their own models removes the owner's accountability.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because review adds rigor. But pre-approving acceptances would put IS audit inside a decision it must later assess independently.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a stricter bar sounds safer. But overall accuracy can hide costly error types, such as missed threats, and later drift; owners still could not judge what they accept.

tips: Eliminate: A has builders accept risk for their own models, and C puts IS audit inside a decision it must later assess.
Final two: B beats D because a higher accuracy bar still hides error types and drift; role-based training equips owners to judge the risks they accept.
Exam cue: when owners accept AI risk on one accuracy number, recommend role-based training so they can judge error types and drift themselves.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Evidence for likelihood
questions.question: An export credit agency rates its screening model's harm as unlikely after a complaint-free year, but declined applicants learn neither that a model screened them nor why. Which question MOST matters to the IS auditor?

options.A: Whether applicants could ever spot an error by the screening model
options.B: Whether the screening model's hosting provider was audited this year
options.C: Whether the model's own developers set the likelihood rating
options.D: Whether the agency is insured against claims by rejected applicants

questions.key_concept: AI errors are often invisible to the people affected, so an absence of complaints is weak evidence that harm is unlikely.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the cited evidence could and could not have detected before accepting the rating it supports.
questions.correct_explanation: Applicants learn neither that a model screened them nor why they were declined, so they cannot recognize or challenge its errors. No complaints is therefore weak evidence of low likelihood; error rates must be measured directly. Developers setting the rating, option C, is the runner-up: independence matters, but an independent rater relying on the same silence would make the same mistake.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because hosting security is a familiar control. But a secure, audited host says nothing about how often the model screens applicants wrongly.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because self-rating weakens evidence. But an independent rater relying on the same silence would reach the same flawed rating.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because insurance limits losses. But insurance is a response to risk, not evidence about how likely the model is to harm applicants.

tips: Eliminate: D asks about insurance, a response rather than evidence of likelihood, and B asks about hosting security, which says nothing about wrong screening decisions.
Final two: A beats C because silence from people who cannot see the model proves nothing; an independent rater using that silence would err the same way.
Exam cue: when an AI risk rating rests on a lack of complaints, ask whether the people affected could ever have noticed the error.
