questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Changes in who is affected
questions.question: A digital bank's AI budgeting coach was risk-assessed for adult customers; the unchanged model will now be offered in a teen account for ages 13 to 17. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the bank keep the adult assessment, as the model is unchanged
options.B: Have the risk owner test the coach's advice on sample teen accounts
options.C: Have marketing add a parental consent screen to the new teen account
options.D: Have the risk owner reassess the coach's risks for teenage users

questions.key_concept: AI risk assessments are tied to a use and its affected people; a new user group, especially minors, triggers reassessment before launch.
questions.pre_read: Notice what changed since the original assessment, and ask whether that assessment still describes the people affected.
questions.correct_explanation: The original assessment weighed harm to adults. The model is unchanged, but teenagers differ in how they read and act on money advice, and the coach's outputs, data use and safeguards were never judged for them, so the risk owner must reassess before launch. Testing advice on teen accounts, option B, is the runner-up: it is needed, but the reassessment decides which harms and criteria the tests must cover.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because no model change was made. But risk depends on the use and the people affected; teenagers are a group the adult assessment never weighed.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because testing shows how the coach treats teens. But tests need criteria, and only a reassessment of harms to minors sets what to test.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because minors often need parental consent. But choosing a control before the risks are reassessed may miss harms consent cannot address.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps an assessment written for adults though the people affected have changed, and C picks a control before the risks are known.
Final two: D beats B because a new group of affected people triggers reassessment, which then sets the criteria the teen tests must use.
Exam cue: when an AI system reaches a new group of people, especially minors, expect the risk owner to reassess before launch.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Setting AI tolerances
questions.question: A legal aid charity's board states a low appetite for its eligibility-screening model wrongly rejecting people who qualify for help. Which tolerance would the IS auditor consider BEST for senior management to set within it?

options.A: At least 95% overall accuracy on the screening model's held-out test data
options.B: Caseworker review of each rejection to find applicants who qualify
options.C: No more than 1 in 100 qualifying applicants screened out each month
options.D: Monthly drift in the model's input data kept below an agreed limit

questions.key_concept: A tolerance turns appetite into a measurable limit on the harm itself; overall accuracy can stay high while that harm grows.
questions.pre_read: Ask which option could actually tell management when the board's appetite is being breached.
questions.correct_explanation: A tolerance sets a measurable limit, within appetite, on the harm the board named: people who qualify being wrongly rejected. A monthly cap on such rejections can be monitored and escalated. Overall accuracy, option A, is the runner-up: it is measurable, but it blends all errors, so it can stay at 95% while far more qualifying applicants are screened out.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it is precise and measurable. But overall accuracy mixes all errors, so it can hold steady while qualifying applicants are wrongly rejected.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because review catches people wrongly rejected. But it is a control that reduces the harm; a tolerance is the measurable limit that control must keep it within.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because drift is a real AI risk signal. But input drift is an early warning, not a limit on the wrongful rejections the board named.

tips: Eliminate: B is a control that reduces wrongful rejections rather than a limit on them, and D tracks input drift, an early warning rather than the harm itself.
Final two: C beats A because a tolerance limits the named harm directly; overall accuracy can stay high while wrongful rejections rise.
Exam cue: a good AI tolerance measures the harm in the appetite statement, not a general model metric like accuracy.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Multi-model decisions
questions.question: An Australian immigration service runs visa applications through three models; a flag from any one sends a case toward refusal, and each meets its own wrongful-flag tolerance. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Applicants wrongly flagged may not know which model flagged them
options.B: Wrongful flags across all three models together may exceed appetite
options.C: The three models may be retrained on different schedules
options.D: Each model's tolerance may be stricter than the appetite requires

questions.key_concept: When several models feed one decision, their errors combine; tolerances must also cover the end-to-end outcome for the people affected.
questions.pre_read: Follow one applicant through every model, and ask how the chances of a wrong flag add up along the way.
questions.correct_explanation: Because a flag from any one model pushes a case toward refusal, an applicant faces three chances of a wrongful flag. Each model can meet its own tolerance while the combined rate is higher, up to the sum of all three rates, and per-model limits would never show it. Unclear sources of flags, option A, is the runner-up: it weakens appeals, but it does not show whether combined harm stays within appetite.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because applicants need to know what to appeal. But transparency helps challenge one case; it does not show whether combined wrongful flags stay within appetite.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because retraining is a change to control. But differing schedules are a change-management detail; they do not reveal the combined error rate.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tolerances can seem meant to equal appetite. But tolerances sit within it, so stricter limits are normal and help keep combined wrongful flags in bounds.

tips: Eliminate: C is a change-management detail, and D treats tolerances set inside appetite as a flaw, though that is how tolerances work; neither shows combined wrongful flags.
Final two: B beats A because separate tolerances can each be met while combined wrongful flags exceed appetite; transparency helps appeals, not measurement.
Exam cue: when models are chained into one decision, check that someone measures the end-to-end error for the people affected, not just each model.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Vendor exit and continuity
questions.question: A veterinary diagnostics lab licenses a vendor's AI model that reads blood smears; the continuity clause escrows the model's source code if the vendor fails. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Raise the penalty the vendor pays if the model service fails
options.B: Require the vendor's annual controls report covering its data centers
options.C: Test the escrow release process with the escrow agent every year
options.D: Extend escrow to the trained model files and their configuration

questions.key_concept: Source code alone cannot rebuild a trained model; AI continuity needs the trained model files, configuration and, where possible, data.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the lab would actually need to keep reading smears if the vendor disappeared tomorrow.
questions.correct_explanation: A model's behavior lives in its trained parameters, not only in its code; rebuilding it from code would need the original training data, compute and expertise, and the result would likely still differ. Escrow must cover the trained model files and configuration. Testing the release process, option C, is the runner-up: it proves the escrow agent can release what is held, but what is held cannot run the lab's tests.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because penalties motivate vendors. But money after a failure does not keep the lab's blood tests running.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because controls reports are standard vendor assurance. But data center controls say nothing about whether the lab could run the model if the vendor failed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because untested escrow often fails. But a smooth release of source code alone still leaves the lab without a working trained model.

tips: Eliminate: B covers the vendor's data centers rather than continuity of the model, and A pays compensation after failure without keeping the tests running.
Final two: D beats C because testing release of source code proves nothing if code cannot rebuild the trained model the lab depends on.
Exam cue: for AI continuity, the asset to protect is the trained model and its configuration, not just the code that built it.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Vendors using other AI providers
questions.question: A Bahraini wealth manager's reporting vendor now sends client portfolio data to another firm's language model, under that firm's standard terms, to draft commentary. What should the IS auditor consider MOST important to confirm?

options.A: Whether the model provider may keep or train on client data
options.B: Whether the vendor's controls report now covers the model provider
options.C: Whether the vendor encrypts client data sent to the model provider
options.D: Whether the vendor accepts liability for the commentary's content

questions.key_concept: When a vendor passes data to another AI provider, first confirm whether that provider may retain or train on it; accountability stays with the buyer.
questions.pre_read: Trace where the client data goes next, and ask what the new party is allowed to do with it.
questions.correct_explanation: Client data now reaches a fourth party, on its standard terms, outside the original due diligence. Many model providers' standard terms let them keep inputs or use them to improve their models, which could expose confidential portfolios far beyond the original purpose. Controls-report coverage, option B, is the runner-up: it matters for assurance, but such reports cover the provider's environment, not whether its terms permit training on client data.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because controls reports are standard vendor assurance. But they cover operations and security, not whether the provider's terms let it keep or train on client data.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because encryption protects data in transit. But it secures delivery; it does not limit what the provider may do with data once received.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because commentary errors could mislead clients. But accountability for client communications stays with the wealth manager; a liability clause cannot transfer it.

tips: Eliminate: D seeks to transfer accountability, which stays with the wealth manager, and C protects data in transit without limiting what the provider may do with it.
Final two: A beats B because the first question is what the provider may do with client data; controls reports cover its environment, not its terms of use.
Exam cue: when AI adds a party to the data flow, ask first whether that party may keep or train on the data, then how it is protected.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Data quality for training
questions.question: A bus operator will redesign routes with a demand model trained on its smartphone app's trip logs, which the data owner has checked as complete and accurate. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The app's trip records used for training may not be encrypted
options.B: Riders' habits may shift once the redesigned routes begin
options.C: Riders who never use the app are absent from the training data
options.D: The quality checks were run by the data owner, not independently

questions.key_concept: Data can be complete and accurate yet unrepresentative; quality rules for training data must ask who is missing from it.
questions.pre_read: Separate how correct the records are from what the records cover, then judge each option against both.
questions.correct_explanation: Records can be complete and accurate for app users while leaving out every rider who pays cash or has no smartphone, often older or lower-income people. Routes planned from that data may serve them worse. Quality rules must cover representativeness. Independent checks, option D, are the runner-up: independence strengthens evidence, but checking completeness and accuracy again would not reveal who is missing.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because trip data needs protection. But encryption is a security control; it does not change who the training data leaves out.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because habits change with new routes. But that is a later monitoring question; the data is skewed before any route changes.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because owners checking their own data is weaker evidence. But an independent check of completeness and accuracy would still miss riders the app never records.

tips: Eliminate: A is a security control that leaves the data's coverage unchanged, and B is a later monitoring question, while the skew exists now.
Final two: C beats D because rechecking completeness and accuracy, however independently, cannot show riders the app never captured; representativeness is a separate test.
Exam cue: complete and accurate is not the same as representative; ask who never appears in the data the model learned from.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Reusing operational data
questions.question: A Portuguese toll-road operator's data scientists are training a model predicting each commuter's daily route from plate-camera records collected for billing, saying the model keeps no plate numbers. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the team pseudonymize plate numbers before training continues
options.B: Have the data owner decide whether billing data may train this model
options.C: Have the data owner catalog the billing records' lineage
options.D: Have IT restrict the model's training set to data scientists

questions.key_concept: Data collected for one purpose cannot be reused to train a model until its owner approves the new purpose under the collection terms.
questions.pre_read: Compare why the data was collected with what it is now being used for, and ask who can approve the difference.
questions.correct_explanation: The records were collected to bill drivers, so training a model to predict each commuter's route is a new purpose, whatever the model keeps: its predictions describe identifiable people, and models can memorize training records. The data owner must decide, with privacy advice, whether that purpose is permitted before training goes on. Recording lineage, option C, is the runner-up: it documents the data's source, but a record does not make the use permitted.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it lowers identification risk. But route patterns can still point to individuals, and pseudonymizing protects data without deciding whether the new use is allowed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because lineage is core data governance. But recording where the data came from does not decide whether training on it is allowed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because limiting access reduces exposure. But it secures the training set without deciding whether the data may be used to train this model.

tips: Eliminate: D secures the training set without settling whether it may be used, and A pseudonymizes plates, though routes still identify drivers and protecting data does not decide its use.
Final two: B beats C because lineage records the data's source but cannot approve its use; the data owner must first decide whether billing data may train this model.
Exam cue: data held for one purpose is not free to train any model, whatever the builders say the model keeps; expect the data owner to approve the new purpose first.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Customer records in prompts
questions.question: A seafood exporter's support copilot sends each customer's full account record, bank details included, to a hosted language model with every query, though most concern shipment status. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have IT encrypt traffic between the copilot and the model provider
options.B: Have the business owner pseudonymize customer names in each prompt
options.C: Have the vendor mask bank details in the copilot's answers
options.D: Have the business owner limit prompts to fields each task needs

questions.key_concept: Privacy by design for AI starts with minimization: prompts should carry only the personal data the task needs.
questions.pre_read: Follow the customer data from the copilot to the hosted model, and ask what each kind of query actually requires.
questions.correct_explanation: Every query sends bank details the hosted model never needs to answer a shipment question, so they leave the exporter's control each time. Privacy by design starts with minimization: send only the fields each task needs. Pseudonymizing names, option B, is the runner-up: it lowers identifiability, but bank details and the rest of the record still reach the provider.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because encryption protects customer data. But it guards the data on the way; the provider still receives every bank detail in full.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because pseudonymizing is a privacy technique. But bank details and the rest of the record still reach the provider, though the query never needs them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because output filters are a common AI safeguard. But masking answers does nothing about the full records sent in every prompt.

tips: Eliminate: A encrypts data in transit, but the provider still receives it, and C masks answers while full records still go out in every prompt.
Final two: D beats B because sending only the fields a task needs keeps bank details from the provider; pseudonymizing names still sends them.
Exam cue: privacy by design for AI starts with the prompt; expect data minimization before filters, encryption or vendor promises.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Assessing a chatbot's privacy
questions.question: A Kenyan wildlife charity's privacy impact assessment for its donor chatbot was completed by the security team and covers only encryption and access to stored records. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the privacy officer extend it to prompts, outputs and logs
options.B: Have the vendor certify that the chatbot complies with privacy laws
options.C: Have the security team add penetration tests of the chatbot
options.D: Have the security team encrypt chat logs, prompts and stored records

questions.key_concept: A privacy impact assessment for AI covers personal data in prompts, outputs and logs, and is owned by privacy roles, not only security.
questions.pre_read: List every place donors' personal data can enter or leave the chatbot, then compare that list with what the assessment covers.
questions.correct_explanation: Donors may type personal details into the chatbot, its answers can reveal them, and chat logs keep them. A privacy impact assessment must cover purpose, consent, retention and those flows, and privacy roles own it. Encrypting chats and records, option D, is the runner-up: it notices the logs, but it treats privacy as security and still skips purpose, retention and outputs.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because certification sounds conclusive. But a vendor's claim is an input, and it cannot assess how this charity uses donors' data.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because testing finds weaknesses. But penetration tests are a security control; they do not assess how donors' personal data is used.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it extends protection to chats. But encryption guards against outsiders; it does not assess purpose, retention or what the chatbot reveals.

tips: Eliminate: C adds security testing to a privacy gap, and B relies on a vendor's claim, which cannot assess the charity's own use of donor data.
Final two: A beats D because privacy needs purpose, retention and output checks owned by privacy roles; encrypting logs is still a security answer.
Exam cue: when a privacy assessment of AI covers only security controls, expect the privacy officer to extend it to prompts, outputs and logs.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Releasing a fine-tuned model
questions.question: A funeral-services group fine-tuned a generative model on bereaved families' past emails to draft replies. Before release, which evidence would BEST show the IS auditor whether the model reveals families' personal details?

options.A: The vendor's statement that its base model protects personal details
options.B: The output filter's settings for blocking phone numbers and addresses
options.C: Results of extraction tests probing for memorized family details
options.D: Confirmation that the families' emails were deleted after fine-tuning

questions.key_concept: Fine-tuned models can memorize training text; tests that try to extract it show whether personal data could leak in outputs.
questions.pre_read: Ask where families' details could still exist after training, and which evidence actually probes that place.
questions.correct_explanation: Fine-tuning on distinctive personal text such as families' emails raises the chance the model memorizes and repeats details. Extraction tests that prompt the model to reproduce training text give the most direct evidence of whether it leaks. The output filter's settings, option B, are the runner-up: a filter helps, but settings show intent, not behavior, and pattern blocking misses names and causes of death.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the vendor built the base model. But its statement covers the base model, not memorization from the group's own fine-tuning data.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because filters are a common output control. But settings show what was configured, not what leaks; names and causes of death match no phone-number pattern.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because deleting source data seems final. But a model keeps what it memorized during fine-tuning, so deletion says nothing about its outputs.

tips: Eliminate: D deletes the source but not what the model memorized, and A covers the vendor's base model, not the group's fine-tuning on families' emails.
Final two: C beats B because extraction tests show what the model actually reveals; filter settings show intent and miss details that fit no pattern.
Exam cue: to judge whether a generative model leaks training data, prefer tests that try to extract it over settings, deletions or vendor claims.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Erasure requests and trained models
questions.question: A podcast app's data team concluded by itself that reviews erased at users' request, a tiny share of its generative model's training data, need no model action. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the model owner order retraining after every erasure request
options.B: Have the model owner decide, with the privacy officer confirming
options.C: Have IT confirm the users' reviews were deleted from every system
options.D: Have the data team record its reasoning in the erasure log

questions.key_concept: Whether erasure requires model action is the model owner's decision, confirmed by the privacy officer; a small share of data does not rule out memorization.
questions.pre_read: Ask who should own a decision about a legal duty, and whether the reason given actually holds for generative models.
questions.correct_explanation: Generative models can memorize even data that appears in few training examples, so a tiny share is no proof the reviews are gone. Whether to retrain, filter outputs or record low risk is the model owner's decision, with the privacy officer confirming it meets the legal duty. Recording the reasoning, option D, is the runner-up: it creates a trail, but the flawed decision stays with the builders.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because retraining removes the data. But a blanket rule is costly and not always needed; each case calls for weighing retraining, output filtering or recorded low risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because complete deletion seems to answer the request. But deleting source reviews does not remove what the trained model may have memorized.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because documented decisions can be reviewed. But recording a flawed share-based argument leaves the builders deciding a legal duty without the model owner or the privacy officer.

tips: Eliminate: A sets blanket retraining for every request, though each case needs weighing, and C deletes source reviews, which does not touch what the model memorized.
Final two: B beats D because memorization can occur even for rare examples, so the decision needs the accountable model owner and the privacy officer, not the builders' recorded judgment.
Exam cue: after an erasure request, the model owner decides what happens to trained models, with the privacy officer confirming; data share alone proves nothing.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Replacing a scoring method
questions.question: A Moroccan development agency replaced its points-based grant scoring with a model 6% more accurate at predicting business survival; rejected applicants are entitled to reasons. Which question should the IS auditor consider MOST important?

options.A: Whether the model can explain each decision in terms people understand
options.B: Whether the agency's systems can score applicants as fast as before
options.C: Whether the model's 6% gain held on data kept back from builders
options.D: Whether reasons given under the old points rules were archived

questions.key_concept: Trustworthy-AI characteristics trade off; a gain in accuracy cannot override an explainability requirement owed to the people affected.
questions.pre_read: Read the stem for any duty owed to the people affected, then test each option against it.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST notes that accuracy and interpretability can trade off. Here the agency owes every rejected applicant reasons, so a more accurate model that cannot produce meaningful ones fails a requirement, whatever its gain. Confirming the 6% on unseen data, option C, is the runner-up: it tests whether the gain is real, but a real gain still would not meet the duty to explain.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because complex models need capacity. But speed is an operational question; it does not affect what the agency owes rejected applicants.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because claimed gains need independent proof. But even a confirmed 6% gain would not let the agency give rejected applicants the reasons they are owed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because records support later review. But archiving past reasons concerns old decisions; it does not show the new model can explain new ones.

tips: Eliminate: B is an operational speed question, and D archives reasons for past decisions; neither shows the new model can explain its rejections.
Final two: A beats C because a confirmed accuracy gain still cannot meet the duty to give reasons; explainability here is a requirement, not a preference.
Exam cue: when a more accurate model replaces an explainable one, check first whether the people affected can still get the explanations they are owed.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Criteria for AI principles
questions.question: An Estonian ferry operator's AI principles say its booking chatbot must be transparent. Which owner-set criterion would BEST let the IS auditor test that principle?

options.A: The vendor publishes an annual transparency report on its model
options.B: Chatbot fare answers match the published fare table in 99% of tests
options.C: The chatbot is designed to be open and honest with passengers
options.D: Every chat starts by telling passengers they are talking to AI

questions.key_concept: A principle becomes auditable when owners state it as an observable criterion that measures that principle in this use, such as disclosure in every chat.
questions.pre_read: For each option, ask whether a tester could check it in this chatbot, and which trustworthy-AI quality it would actually measure.
questions.correct_explanation: Transparency in the NIST framework concerns what information about an AI system is available to the people interacting with it. A rule that every chat opens by saying the passenger is talking to AI is specific to this use and can be checked chat by chat. Fare accuracy, option B, is the runner-up: it is testable, but it measures validity, not transparency.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it is published and independent of the operator. But it describes the vendor's model in general, not what passengers are told in this chatbot.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is specific and testable. But matching fares tests whether answers are valid, not whether passengers know they are dealing with AI.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it sounds like the principle. But a design aim restates the principle; it gives a tester nothing measurable to check.

tips: Eliminate: C restates the principle without anything to measure, and A is the vendor's general report, which cannot be checked against this chatbot.
Final two: D beats B because transparency concerns what people are told about the AI; fare accuracy is testable but measures validity, a different characteristic.
Exam cue: a testable criterion must also measure the right characteristic; ask which trustworthy-AI quality each option actually tests.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Uses outside a law's scope
questions.question: Legal counsel finds a supermarket chain's pricing model outside a new AI law, so the AI governance committee proposes dropping checks for unfair prices in low-income areas. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Replace the checks by removing income data from the model's inputs
options.B: Drop the checks, since the law defines what shoppers are owed
options.C: Keep the checks as part of managing the model's risk to shoppers
options.D: Have counsel recheck the law's scope at each annual compliance review

questions.key_concept: Legal compliance is a floor: an AI use outside one law still answers to other laws, the organization's principles and its risk appetite.
questions.pre_read: Ask what besides this one law should govern how the model treats shoppers.
questions.correct_explanation: Being outside one AI law removes that law's duties, not the risk that the model charges low-income neighborhoods more, which other laws and the chain's own risk management may still need to address. Removing income data, option A, is the runner-up: it looks like a fix, but store location and other inputs can stand in for income, so only outcome checks reveal unfair prices.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because removing income data seems to remove the bias. But store location and other inputs can stand in for income, so only outcome checks show unfair prices.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because counsel has confirmed scope. But one law is a floor; other laws and the chain's own risk limits still apply to unfair pricing.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because laws change and scope can shift. But rechecking scope still treats one law as the only reason to test for unfair prices.

tips: Eliminate: B treats one law as the whole standard, though it is only a floor, and D keeps tracking legal scope while the pricing harm goes unchecked.
Final two: C beats A because other inputs, such as store location, can stand in for income; only checking actual prices shows whether low-income areas pay more.
Exam cue: being outside one AI law does not end the duty to manage harm; expect checks to follow risk to people, not just legal scope.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Deciding which laws apply
questions.question: A cosmetics retailer's app uses a vendor's skin-analysis model, and the vendor says a new AI law's high-risk rules do not apply. Who should the IS auditor expect to hold PRIMARY responsibility for that judgment?

options.A: The retailer's AI governance committee, voting on the vendor's view
options.B: The retailer's legal counsel, advised by the model owner
options.C: The IS auditor, after testing the model's controls in the app
options.D: The vendor, which built the model and knows its design best

questions.key_concept: Whether an AI law's duties apply to the organization depends on its own use and market; that is a legal judgment for its counsel.
questions.pre_read: Separate who built the model from who uses it, and ask who should judge what the law requires of the retailer.
questions.correct_explanation: Applicability turns on how, where and for whom the retailer uses the model, which the retailer knows best, so it is a legal judgment for the retailer's counsel, informed by the model owner's description of the use. The AI governance committee, option A, is the runner-up: it approves high-impact uses and acts on the answer, but a vote cannot replace a legal judgment.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the committee governs AI uses. But applicability is a legal judgment; the committee acts on counsel's answer rather than voting on a vendor's view.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because IS auditors assess compliance. But applicability is a legal judgment for counsel; the IS auditor later tests the mapping and evidence rather than deciding applicability.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the vendor knows the model's design. But the retailer's own duties depend on its use, so the vendor's view is an input to counsel, not the judgment.

tips: Eliminate: D leaves applicability to the vendor, whose view is only an input, and C has the IS auditor making a judgment it must later assess.
Final two: B beats A because applicability is a legal judgment about the retailer's own use; the committee acts on that answer rather than replacing it.
Exam cue: who decides whether an AI law applies? Legal counsel, using the owner's account of the use; vendors advise and IS auditors test.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. A certified AI management system
questions.question: A dental-supplies distributor holds ISO/IEC 42001 certification for its AI management system, and its board asks whether the NIST AI RMF adds anything for its clinic credit-limit model. What is the IS auditor's BEST answer?

options.A: It repeats what the certificate already shows about model risk
options.B: It is a US legal duty the certificate does not yet meet
options.C: It is written for generative AI rather than credit-limit models
options.D: It guides mapping and measuring this model's own risks

questions.key_concept: A management-system certificate covers the process within its scope; the voluntary, use-case-agnostic NIST AI RMF can still guide model-level risk work.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the certificate's auditors actually examined, then compare that with what each option claims about the NIST framework.
questions.correct_explanation: Certification shows the distributor's AI management system meets ISO/IEC 42001 within its scope; it does not test how this model behaves. The NIST AI RMF, voluntary and use-case agnostic, adds detailed Map and Measure guidance at model level: context, affected clinics, tolerances and testing. That the certificate already covers model risk, option A, is the runner-up: it is a common reading, but certification covers the management system, not the model.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because certification involves independent auditors. But they assess the management system within its scope, not how this credit-limit model treats clinics.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because NIST is a US government body. But NIST describes the AI RMF as voluntary; it guides risk work and creates no legal duty.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because NIST also publishes a generative AI profile. But the AI RMF itself is use-case agnostic and covers predictive models like this one.

Final two: D beats A because a management-system certificate shows how AI is governed within its scope, not how well this model's risks were mapped and measured.

questions.question: A ship classification society using the NIST AI RMF has tested its inspection-scheduling model for bias and robustness, but never documented its intended use, affected parties or tolerances. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the model owner define the context of use before more testing
options.B: Have the model owner choose responses to the issues tests found
options.C: Have the society seek external certification of its AI management system
options.D: Have the team extend robustness testing to more attack types

questions.key_concept: In the NIST AI RMF, Map outcomes such as intended use, affected parties and tolerances are the basis for judging Measure results and Manage responses.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a tester needs to know before deciding whether a bias or robustness result is good enough.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST describes Map outcomes as the basis for Measure and Manage: without a documented intended use, affected parties and tolerances, nobody can say which test results matter or what level is acceptable. The model owner should document that context first, with tolerances from senior management. Choosing risk responses, option B, is the runner-up: acting on findings seems decisive, but responses chosen without tolerances have nothing to aim at.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because findings call for action. But without tolerances and intended use, there is no basis for deciding which findings need a response or how much.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because certification sounds like assurance. But a management-system certificate covers process scope; it does not supply this model's missing context.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because broader testing finds more issues. But more tests without context produce more results nobody can judge against a purpose or tolerance.

tips: Eliminate: D adds tests that still lack a basis for judgment, and C seeks a process certificate, which cannot supply the model's missing context.
Final two: A beats B because responses need tolerances to aim at; Map outcomes are the basis for both Measure and Manage.
Exam cue: in the NIST AI RMF, expect context (intended use, affected people, tolerances) to be set before test results or responses are judged.
